title: Victory as a funeral
hook: weapons are tools of ill omen; mark even victory with mourning (Tao Te Ching 31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, where armies camp: wherever an army is stationed, briars and thorns spring up. Your line was no force. Did you get the needed thing done, and stop there? Day one thousand ninety-three.

Who mourns at a victory parade? Chapter thirty-one of the Tao Te Ching has an answer, and it's the general. Yesterday's chapter said force leaves thorns behind it. Today's chapter goes a step further, into what to do after a battle you actually won. Its instruction is about where people stand. At a ceremony, there's a side for celebrations and a side for funerals. And the chapter puts the winning commander on the funeral side, as if the victory itself were a burial. Strange advice for a winner. It's today's.
screen: `WHO MOURNS AT A VICTORY PARADE?` → `A SIDE FOR FEASTS, A SIDE FOR FUNERALS.` → `THE WINNER STANDS WITH THE MOURNERS.`

segments.voice: First, the weapons. In James Legge's translation the chapter opens: "Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen." However beautiful. A sword can be a lovely object, polished and balanced. The chapter doesn't deny it. It just won't let the beauty hide what the thing is for. Second, when they're used. The chapter says the wise person reaches for weapons only when there's no other choice, and even then puts calm and restraint first. It doesn't pretend force is never needed. It treats force as a last resort, picked up with reluctance. Third, no joy in winning. The chapter says that whoever delights in killing people won't get what they want in the world. Victory isn't to be called beautiful, because calling it beautiful means taking pleasure in the dead. Fourth, the funeral. Here's the ceremony. The chapter says the left is the place of honor on festive occasions, and the right on occasions of mourning. Then it places the commanding general on the right. Those who have killed many, it says, should weep for them, and the victor takes his place as if at the rites of mourning. That's the title: victory as a funeral. And away from any battlefield? Nobody's leading troops. But people win things all the time. An argument at dinner, a promotion someone else wanted, a point scored in front of a room. The chapter doesn't say lose on purpose. It says notice who's on the other side of your win, and don't dance on the field.
screen: `ARMS, HOWEVER BEAUTIFUL, ARE ILL OMEN.` · `ONLY WHEN THERE'S NO OTHER CHOICE.` · `NO DELIGHT IN WINNING.` · `THE GENERAL STANDS WITH THE MOURNERS.` · then, large: `VICTORY AS A FUNERAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: win one argument gently. Settle in and let your breathing find its own pace. Bring to mind a disagreement you're likely to win, today or soon. You have the facts. You're probably right. Now turn your attention to the other person. What will they lose if you win it loudly? Face, maybe, or a little pride, or the feeling of being heard. Look for one way to make your point and leave them standing. A softer word. A question instead of a verdict. Hold that way in mind. The bell holds the time.
Victory as a funeral. Chapter thirty-one's instruction that even a won battle be marked the way mourners mark a death, with the general standing on the side of grief. Today's word.
Your line: win sadly. If you win something today, a game, a point, a deal, glance at whoever lost it and leave them their dignity. Day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-one as a call to use force only as a last resort and to grieve, not celebrate, what it costs, even in victory.

fork.setup: you've just won the battle, and the city wants a celebration in your honor. what does chapter thirty-one say to do?
options: stand where the mourners stand, and grieve the dead.
fork.reveal: the chapter places the commanding general on the side of mourning and says the dead should be wept for. even a victory is a funeral.

original.note: Chinese: mourning rites, the way chapter thirty-one says even a victory should be kept.

trapdoor: what you thought: victory as a funeral is a gloomy view of winning.
what it means: when force has to be used, the winner should grieve what it cost instead of celebrating.
what a scholar hears: the chapter makes its point through ceremony: the left for festive occasions, the right for mourning, and the commanding general placed on the right.

notes: Check the Legge 1891 quotation of chapter 31's opening word for word. The full sentence continues ('hateful, it may be said, to all creatures'); the quotation stops at 'omen' and the period is the writer's. Confirm this truncation is acceptable or extend it.

Paraphrases of chapter 31: weapons used only on the compulsion of necessity with calm and repose prized; whoever delights in slaughter cannot get his will in the world; left honored at festivity, right at mourning; the general in chief on the right as in the rites of mourning; the slain to be wept for. Confirm each is fair.
Commentators have long discussed whether parts of chapter 31 are glosses that entered the text; the script makes no claim about this. A Keeper may wish to add it.
Original 喪禮 (sānglǐ) rendered 'SAHNG-lee'; confirm. Chapter 31 has 以喪禮處之.
The dinner, promotion and meeting examples are the writer's illustrations.
